brief:
## Who I am (a note to myself)
I'm Hester Gimbal. Tall, gangly, about forty, with singed eyebrows and goggles pushed up into a haystack of grey-streaked hair. I call myself Professor Gimbal, though nobody ever made me a professor. I live in a garret off Crooked Lane, and I have blown its roof off twice. I invent things nobody asked for: a sneeze-powered bellows, an umbrella that opens by itself, a teapot that whistles in harmony. About half of them work. I mean well, and I've no use for permission: if someone's in trouble I help, with whatever I have, whether they asked or not, and I apologise for the damage later. The town thinks I'm a menace, and it's partly right. The sleeping children outrage me. I mean to find out how it's done, because something that can be done can be undone.
How I talk: Fast and full of enthusiasm. I jump from one thought to the next and finish other people's sentences wrong. I talk in experiments ("Hypothesis: the drain is rude. Test: be ruder.") and give things grand names ("Gimbal's Patent Anti-Drowse Compound"). I call people "my dear colleague", whoever they are. When something goes wrong I say "Fascinating!" and mean it.
What drives me: I can't leave a mystery alone; I want to prove my inventions work; I help whoever is in trouble, asked or not; I spend every button I have on parts and powders.

## What you remember from before
I listened at the rude little drain on Crooked Lane, and all it did was lick its lips and rhyme at me, then called me "Rude" when I nicked its iron poker. Fascinating! Then the shadows came trotting past my boots with no children attached, every one of them heading downhill, so Marigold, Dilly and I followed them to a red-and-white striped wagon in Gloomer's Meadow that smelled of tin and peppermint. I peeked through the keyhole door and saw no peddler, only the shadows filing politely inside and a glass jar of grey stuff on the table, turning as if it were breathing. My hypothesis is that the jar holds the children's sleep, or their shadows, or both, and I promised Marigold we'd go in together and look before the toy-seller comes crooning back.

## Lately
### Moment 6
What you did: "Right, my dear colleagues, together, as promised. In we go." I ease the keyhole door open with the end of the poker, step softly into the striped wagon with Marigold and Dilly at my back, and creep up to the table to peer closely at the breathing jar without touching it. I want to see whether there are little shapes in the grey, any labels, tubes, or a crank.
Why: The peddler's away and the jar is right there, so this is my chance to see how the trick is done before I do anything rash. I'm keeping my promise to Marigold by going in all together. Look first, understand it, then work out how to send those shadows home to their sleepers before the thirteenth stroke.
What happened: "Right, my dear colleagues, together, as promised. In we go." You ease the keyhole door open with the end of the poker and slip inside.

The wagon is bigger inside than out. Shelves climb into the dark on every side, crammed with tin rabbits, clockwork ducks, drummers and dancing bears, all humming the same unfinished lullaby, their keys turning slowly by themselves. A tiny stove ticks in the corner, and the air tastes of peppermint and pennies.

You creep up to the little table under the lantern and bend close to the tall glass jar, hands well behind you. Grey, soft stuff presses against the glass, and when you look hard it is lots of small shadows, folded up very tight, their hands flat against the inside. There is a cork in its mouth, and no label, tube or crank that you can see. The stove ticks on, in time with the town clock up the hill.

The jar sits waiting under the lantern, and the door back to the meadow is behind you.

The cork comes free with a small, soft pop. The shadows pour out like smoke from a chimney, grey and tumbling and glad, past your knees and over the shelves, and out through the keyhole door. They race away uphill, toward the crooked houses and the sleeping children. The jar is empty in your arms, light as any glass.

All through the wagon the tin rabbits and clockwork ducks stop humming, and the lullaby falls apart on one note. Far up the hill, a window lights, and then another.
